extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, scientific researchers, and scientific authors (aspiring or practising writers of long-form natural history/science works)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for conducting empirical natural-history research and for composing, editing, and publishing long-form scientific works based on Darwin's autobiographical reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baconian collection of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Work on 'true Baconian principles'—collect facts without theory and only later attempt synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin states he collected facts 'on a wholesale scale' without starting from theory, particularly about domesticated productions and natural variation. The guidance implies exhaustive, inductive data-gathering (printed enquiries, conversations, reading) before committing to a theoretical account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record counter-evidence immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a published fact, new observation or thought occurs which is opposed to your general results, 'make a memorandum of it without fail and at once.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasises permanently noting opposing facts so they aren't forgotten; this practice reduced unanticipated objections and ensured few objections were raised that he hadn't at least noticed and attempted to answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a diary and extensive notebooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a little diary and numerous notebooks/portfolios to record observations and notes over a career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin kept daily diaries and many portfolios; he opened his first notebook for variation in July 1837. Regular note-taking is presented as foundational to later synthesis and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organised, classified reference system
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise references and abstracts in labelled portfolios with classified indexes for rapid retrieval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He keeps 'thirty to forty large portfolios' and writes indices at book ends or makes separate abstracts, then composes a general classified index before beginning a subject, enabling immediate access to collected information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive literature abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Read widely and abstract relevant literature and journals; make abstracts of books and papers that concern your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin lists extensive reading and abstracting as core to his industry; he often wrote out abstracts of books he did not own and compiled lists of facts from many sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative planning and outlining
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan books by making a rudest outline, then a larger one, then expand headings before full writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He first sketches two- to three-page outlines, then several-page outlines where a word or phrase may stand for an entire discussion, and subsequently expands and transfers headings—this iterative enlargement guides organisation of large works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce larger manuscripts then abstract them
rubrics_metrics.description: Work on a large-scale manuscript and then produce an abstract/condensed sketch for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin wrote on a scale three or four times as extensive as the final 'Origin' and then abstracted it; he attributes some success to having earlier written condensed sketches and abstracts that let him select striking facts and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and emphasise the most striking facts
rubrics_metrics.description: From extensive material, select the more striking facts and conclusions for presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin credits selecting striking facts (enabled by prior sketches and abstracts) with aiding the book's success; implies importance of editorial selection to make an argument persuasive and readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and answer objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate objections—collect criticisms and attempt to answer them in your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He notes that by recording opposing facts and thoughts he could address many objections; this is presented as an explicit method to strengthen arguments and reduce successful attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain new views at considerable length
rubrics_metrics.description: New or radical views should be explained at length to arouse public and professional attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin observes that his and Wallace's joint early publications attracted little attention, and that Professor Haughton judged 'all that was new... false'—Darwin concludes that new views require substantial explanation to be taken seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate concision for readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an appropriate size and level of condensation for the intended audience; moderate size can aid reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin felt the moderate size of the 'Origin' (partly forced by Wallace's essay) made the book more readable and aided its success; overly large treatments may deter readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify accidental observations with tests and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not act on accidental observations until repeated tests and crucial experiments confirm their significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the entrapment of insects by Drosera led to controlled tests (leaves in fluids) that demonstrated a nitrogen-response; Darwin stresses repeating and designing crucial tests before building a large project from a chance finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise experimental tests to distinguish explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Design decisive experiments that can discriminate between competing hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He describes devising crucial tests (e.g., for Drosera) and devising experiments to test theories (e.g., on cross- vs self-fertilisation), indicating that experiments should be targeted to resolve the core question and not merely be descriptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use long-term and patient observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry out experiments and observations over long periods and with patience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many of Darwin's projects (Cirripedia, Insectivorous Plants, Cross-and Self-Fertilisation) involved years, sometimes decades, of observation and experiment; long delay often improved the quality and completeness of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to abandon or modify hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the mind free to give up any hypothesis as soon as facts are shown to be opposed to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin recounts giving up many first-formed hypotheses; intellectual flexibility and readiness to change position are presented as scientific virtues that avoid dogmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid entanglement in controversies as they often do little good and waste time and temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Lyell's advice, Darwin avoided controversies when possible; this is counsel both for personal preservation and for productive use of time, though he did respond to substantive criticisms when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult and collaborate with knowledgeable peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek the advice and critique of trusted peers and senior colleagues when preparing and publishing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin credits Lyell and Hooker for urging him to publish and advising on presentation; consulting peers can influence timing, scope, and form of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observations of others and acknowledge them
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensively use and incorporate observations made by others, abstracting and integrating them into your synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that many of his books extensively used facts observed by others; he organized, abstracted, and incorporated external observations into his arguments, implying diligent scholarship and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative drafting and revision for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Scribble rough drafts quickly, then correct deliberately; spend significant time on arrangement and expression to achieve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin admits difficulty in expression and describes a working method ('scribble in a vile hand... then correct deliberately') and heavy time spent on arranging matter; the practice yields clearer sentences despite initial messiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record methods of data collation (indexes, abstracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make short indexes of books, write abstracts, and compile classified indexes before beginning writing so factual material is searchable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He creates short indexes and classified indexes, stores abstracts in drawers, and composes a general index to select proper portfolios; this detailed metadata practice supports rigorous referencing and argument construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be industrious and steady in scientific work
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained industry, steady love of natural science, and patience to ponder problems for years are necessary conditions for success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin attributes much of his success to industriousness and the patience to reflect for years; this is framed as a character and work-ethic standard for evaluators of scientific careers.
